title: Best Mechanical Keyboards UK
short: Mechanical keyboards compared by build quality, switch feel and size, from budget compact boards to premium gaming keyboards.
intro: A mechanical keyboard's price mostly buys you build quality and typing feel rather than raw features. This guide compares keyboards tested by RTINGS, which says it has bought and tested 299 keyboards, spanning budget, mid-range, premium and gaming options.

products.name: Q5 Max
products.best_for: Buyers who want a premium full-size keyboard that's fully customisable
products.summary: RTINGS' top pick, with a premium heavyweight aluminium case and top-of-the-line typing quality out of the box. The double gasket-mounted design and internal sound-dampening foam give a softer, cushioned feel, though the pre-lubed stabilizers sounded slightly inconsistent on the unit RTINGS tested.
pros: Top-of-the-line typing quality out of the box
cons: Stabilizers sounded slightly inconsistent on the tested unit

products.name: Node Series
products.best_for: Buyers who want a well-tuned board without paying for an aluminium case
products.key_spec: 75% or full-size, standard or low-profile, wireless, hot-swappable
products.summary: RTINGS' mid-range pick, offering excellent build and typing quality despite an all-plastic construction. Pre-lubed and well-tuned switches and stabilizers give smooth, consistent keystrokes, with a choice of low-profile or standard-profile layouts, though the low-profile version's compressed layout takes some getting used to.
pros: Excellent build and typing quality for the price
Choice of standard or low-profile versions
cons: Low-profile version's compressed layout takes adjustment

products.name: OK-M
products.best_for: Buyers who want a high-quality typing feel without a premium price
products.summary: RTINGS' budget pick, offering a surprisingly similar typing experience to pricier boards despite the lower price. Build quality is good for the price, though the plastic case has a little more flex and the soft gasket mount leans slightly mushy rather than springy.
pros: High-quality typing experience for the price
Compatible with the open-source VIA configurator
cons: Plastic pieces have more flex than pricier boards
Gasket mount leans mushy rather than springy

products.name: RK61
products.best_for: Buyers on a tight budget who want a tiny desk footprint
products.summary: RTINGS' pick for the cheapest usable mechanical keyboard, with a tiny footprint that suits small desks or travel. It supports multi-device Bluetooth pairing and a hot-swappable PCB, though battery life is limited to around 10 hours and there's no dedicated arrow keys or function row.
pros: Tiny footprint for small desks or travel
Hot-swappable PCB for easy switch replacement
cons: No dedicated arrow keys, function row or nav cluster

products.name: 80HE
products.best_for: Competitive gamers who want adjustable actuation and rapid trigger
products.key_spec: TKL (80%), wired, magnetic Hall-effect switches, up to 8000Hz polling
products.summary: RTINGS' top gaming pick, using magnetic switches rather than traditional mechanical ones so you can fine-tune actuation distance and use Rapid Trigger for near-instant key resets. Exceptional latency and input granularity, with a four-year warranty, though the zinc alloy case version costs more than the plastic variant RTINGS recommends instead.
pros: Rapid Trigger and adjustable actuation for competitive play
Analog input suits racing/flight sim games
cons: Zinc alloy case costs more than the recommended plastic version

products.name: Flow 2
products.best_for: Buyers who want the most refined low-profile typing feel
products.key_spec: Low-profile, full aluminium case, multiple switch and size options
products.summary: RTINGS' notable-mention alternative to the NuPhy Node Series for buyers who want more refined materials. It has a full aluminium case and an even more premium out-of-the-box typing experience, available in several sizes including a silent switch option, at a higher price.
pros: More premium typing experience than plastic rivals
cons: More expensive than the plastic NuPhy Node Series

guide.q: What size keyboard should I choose?
guide.a: Full-size and 96% layouts keep a numpad, useful for spreadsheet work. TKL (80%) drops the numpad to save space. 75% keeps arrow keys and a few function keys in a tighter layout. 60% drops almost everything except the core keys, best suited to buyers who don't mind using key combinations for arrows and function keys.

guide.q: What's the difference between linear, tactile and clicky switches?
guide.a: Linear switches move smoothly with no bump, favoured for gaming. Tactile switches have a noticeable bump partway down, popular for typing feel. Clicky switches add an audible click on top of the tactile bump, loved by some typists but often disliked by anyone sharing a room or a call.

guide.q: Is a hot-swappable keyboard worth it?
guide.a: A hot-swappable PCB lets you pull out and replace switches without soldering, so you can try different switch feels or replace a broken switch easily. It's a genuinely useful feature if you think you might want to experiment, and most of the keyboards in this guide include it.

guide.q: Do gaming keyboards need magnetic (Hall-effect) switches?
guide.a: Magnetic switches, like those in the Wooting 80HE here, let you adjust exactly how far a key needs to travel before it registers, and support Rapid Trigger for near-instant repeated inputs. This mainly benefits competitive players in fast-paced games; casual gamers and typists are well served by traditional mechanical switches.
